lesson.menu_desc: Comparing two options out loud, and saying which one wins -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- Two Hotels, One Choice
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Veridiana Sterman Petrilli | Lesson 8 -- Two Hotels, One Choice

listenings.text: I have been booking travel for other people for eleven years, and I can tell you the mistake almost everybody makes. They compare the wrong thing. They open two hotels side by side and they compare the price, because the price is the number the website puts in the biggest letters. But the price is only one line of the bill. The hotel that is forty dollars cheaper is usually further from everything, and if you take two taxis a day for nine days, you have paid the difference three times over. So compare the total, not the rate. My second rule is about reviews. Do not read the best ones and do not read the worst ones. Read the ones in the middle, because those are written by people who are not angry and not in love, and they are the only ones who tell you what the place is actually like on a normal Tuesday. And my third rule is the simplest. Whatever you choose, choose the quieter one. Nobody in the history of travel has ever come home and said the room was too quiet.

Here is something people from outside the United States are often surprised by. In most American beach cities, the difference between one street and the next one is enormous. The block right on the ocean is the loudest, the most expensive and the most crowded, and it is where almost every visitor books. Walk three streets inland and the same room is thirty per cent cheaper, the street is quieter at night, and the beach is still a five-minute walk away. The trade-off is real, but it is smaller than the price difference suggests. The second thing is the shuttle. A lot of the bigger hotels run a free shuttle to the main areas, and it is almost never mentioned on the booking page, only on the hotel's own website. So before you decide that the cheaper hotel is too far, check whether it has a shuttle. Two of the three hotels I stayed in last year did, and I only found out on the second morning.

paras: Two hotels, nine nights, the same week in October. The first one is on the ocean: two hundred and twenty dollars a night, everything within walking distance, and the reviews say it is noisy until about one in the morning. The second one is three streets inland: a hundred and eighty a night, quieter, bigger rooms, and a fifteen-minute walk from the beach. Forty dollars a night, nine nights: three hundred and sixty dollars of difference.

That number is the one everybody looks at, and it is the wrong one. The cheaper hotel is further from the restaurants, so most guests take a taxi in the evening. Two short taxis a day, at about twelve dollars each, is twenty-four dollars, and over nine days that is two hundred and sixteen. The difference is no longer three hundred and sixty. It is a hundred and forty-four, and now the question is a different question: is the quieter room worth sixteen dollars a night?

The reviews are the second trap. The best reviews and the worst reviews are both written by people who are not thinking clearly, one group in love and the other group angry. The reviews in the middle are the useful ones, and in this case they agree with each other: the ocean hotel has the better location and the worse sleep, and the inland hotel is better value for money if you do not mind the walk.

There is one more line, and almost nobody reads it, because it is on the hotel's own site and not on the booking page. The inland hotel runs a free shuttle to the main area every thirty minutes until eleven at night. That single line changes the arithmetic completely: no taxis, the same quiet room, and the walk only matters after eleven. The most expensive hotel is not always the best one, and the cheapest one is almost never the worst. The one that wins is usually the one whose small print somebody actually read.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from two real booking pages for the same week in Miami Beach.

choices: To recommend the cheaper hotel over the more expensive one.
To show that the number on the page is not the number that decides, and what to compare instead.
To explain why hotel reviews cannot be trusted at all.

items.situation: Compare the two hotels on price, in one sentence.
tips: The inland hotel is forty dollars cheaper than the one on the ocean.
Short adjectives take -er plus than: cheaper than, quieter than.

items.situation: Now compare them on convenience, using a long adjective.
tips: The ocean hotel is more convenient than the inland one.
Long adjectives take more. Never more cheaper.

items.situation: Say that one thing is equal, and one thing is not.
tips: The rooms are as clean as each other, but the inland one is not as close to the beach.
As + adjective + as for equal; not as + adjective + as for less.

items.situation: Say which one is the extreme, out of all the hotels you looked at.
tips: The ocean hotel was the most expensive one, and the noisiest.
The superlative takes the: the most expensive, the noisiest.

items.situation: Use the two irregular ones in the same sentence.
tips: The location is better, but the sleep is worse.
Good becomes better and the best; bad becomes worse and the worst.

items.situation: Now compare two real places in your own week, and say which one wins and why.
tips: The gym near the practice is closer, but the one near home is quieter, so I go there more often.
Comparison plus reason: the second half is what makes it a real answer.
